claim: The ongoing coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic is caused by the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), which emerged in central China late 2019.
source: The ongoing coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic is caused by the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), which emerged in central China late 2019 (Zhu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhu et al., 2020, which provides published evidence for the emergence of SARS-CoV-2.

claim: As of October 15, 2020, over 38 million COVID-19 cases have been reported, including over 1 million deaths.
source: Within months, this virus spread globally, and as of October 15, 2020, over 38 million cases have been reported, including over 1 million deaths.
evidence: The claim provides specific epidemiological data as of a specific date, representing factual reporting of case numbers.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is the third zoonotic coronavirus to emerge from animal reservoirs within the past two decades, after SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV.
source: SARS-CoV-2 is the third zoonotic coronavirus to emerge from animal reservoirs within the past two decades, after SARS-CoV and Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV), in 2002 and 2012, respectively (Drosten et al., 2003; Kuiken et al., 2003; Peiris et al., 2003b; Zaki et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting the emergence of SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV.

claim: SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV have not attained sustained human-to-human transmission.
source: In contrast to SARS-CoV-2, SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV have not attained sustained human-to-human transmission.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the transmission characteristics of these coronaviruses.

claim: SARS-CoV-2, SARS-CoV, and MERS-CoV belong to the Betacoronavirus genus.
source: These coronaviruses belong to the Betacoronavirus genus (family Coronaviridae, subfamily Orthocoronavirinae), which is thought to ultimately originate from bats, but can spread to humans via intermediate hosts (Hu et al., 2015; Lau et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and represents established taxonomic classification.

claim: Betacoronaviruses are thought to ultimately originate from bats, but can spread to humans via intermediate hosts.
source: These coronaviruses belong to the Betacoronavirus genus (family Coronaviridae, subfamily Orthocoronavirinae), which is thought to ultimately originate from bats, but can spread to humans via intermediate hosts (Hu et al., 2015; Lau et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting the zoonotic origins of betacoronaviruses.

claim: The coronavirus spike (S) protein is the main glycoprotein incorporated into the viral envelope.
source: Currently, it is largely unknown what factors determine coronavirus transmission to and between humans, but one important determinant may be the coronavirus spike (S) protein, which is the main glycoprotein incorporated into the viral envelope.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about coronavirus structure.

claim: Coronavirus S protein trimers fuse viral and cellular membranes after binding to the entry receptor.
source: This function is executed by S protein trimers, which fuse viral and cellular membranes after binding to the entry receptor (Hulswit et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation describing the mechanism of S protein function.

claim: Coronaviruses can spread from cell to cell when coronavirus S proteins traffic to the plasma membrane of infected cells and fuse with neighboring cells, generating multinucleated giant cells (syncytia).
source: In addition, coronaviruses can spread from cell to cell when coronavirus S proteins traffic to the plasma membrane of infected cells and fuse with neighboring cells, generating multinucleated giant cells (syncytia).
evidence: The claim describes a known mechanism of coronavirus cell-to-cell spread.

claim: Coronavirus S proteins are synthesized in infected cells in a stable and fusion-incompetent form and are activated through cleavage by host proteases.
source: Coronavirus S proteins are synthesized in infected cells in a stable and fusion-incompetent form and are activated through cleavage by host proteases.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about S protein activation.

claim: Cleavage is essential for coronavirus infectivity and can occur in the secretory pathway of infected cells or during viral entry into target cells.
source: Cleavage is essential for coronavirus infectivity and can occur in the secretory pathway of infected cells or during viral entry into target cells (Hulswit et al., 2016; Millet and Whittaker, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations documenting the importance of proteolytic cleavage.

claim: Several groups of host proteases, including type II transmembrane serine proteases, proprotein convertases, and cathepsins, can cleave the S protein.
source: Several groups of host proteases, including type II transmembrane serine proteases (hereafter referred to as serine proteases), proprotein convertases, and cathepsins, can cleave the S protein.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about proteases involved in S protein cleavage.

claim: Specific sites in the S protein regulate protease usage and play an important role in determining cell tropism.
source: Specific sites in the S protein regulate protease usage and therefore play an important role in determining cell tropism. Similarly, tropism can be determined by the availability of proteases that can activate the S protein (Belouzard et al., 2012; Menachery et al., 2020; Millet and Whittaker, 2015; Yang et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting the relationship between protease usage and tropism.

claim: The S protein consists of two domains, the receptor binding (S1) domain and the fusion (S2) domain.
source: The S protein consists of two domains, the receptor binding (S1) domain and the fusion (S2) domain.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about S protein structure.

claim: The S1 and S2 domains are separated by the S1/S2 cleavage site.
source: These domains are separated by the S1/S2 cleavage site, which in some coronaviruses, such as SARS-CoV-2, forms an exposed loop that harbors multiple arginine residues and is therefore referred to as a multibasic cleavage site (MBCS) (Walls et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations describing the S1/S2 cleavage site structure.

claim: In SARS-CoV-2, the S1/S2 cleavage site forms an exposed loop that harbors multiple arginine residues and is referred to as a multibasic cleavage site (MBCS).
source: These domains are separated by the S1/S2 cleavage site, which in some coronaviruses, such as SARS-CoV-2, forms an exposed loop that harbors multiple arginine residues and is therefore referred to as a multibasic cleavage site (MBCS) (Walls et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations describing the MBCS structure in SARS-CoV-2.

claim: Cleavage of the S1/S2 site can occur in secretory systems of infected cells by proprotein convertases, including furin.
source: Cleavage of this site can occur in secretory systems of infected cells by proprotein convertases, including furin.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about S1/S2 cleavage mechanisms.

claim: S1/S2 cleavage does not directly trigger fusion but may facilitate or regulate further cleavage.
source: S1/S2 cleavage does not directly trigger fusion but may facilitate or regulate further cleavage (Park et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation describing the function of S1/S2 cleavage.

claim: A second proteolysis step takes place at the S2′ site within the S2 domain.
source: A second proteolysis step takes place at a more C-terminal site within the S2 domain, notably the S2′ site.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about S protein cleavage sites.

claim: S2′ cleavage occurs after the virus has been released from producing cells and is bound to host cell receptors on receiving cells.
source: S2′ cleavage is thought to occur after the virus has been released from producing cells and is bound to host cell receptors on receiving cells.
evidence: The claim represents established understanding of the timing of S2′ cleavage.

claim: The S2′ site is processed by serine proteases on the plasma membrane or by cathepsins in the endosome.
source: The S2′ site is processed by serine proteases on the plasma membrane or by cathepsins in the endosome.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about proteases that cleave the S2′ site.

claim: S2′ cleavage appears to be crucial for coronavirus infectivity.
source: Whereas S2′ cleavage appears to be crucial for coronavirus infectivity, not all coronaviruses contain a multibasic S1/S2 site and little is known of its function (Hulswit et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: Not all coronaviruses contain a multibasic S1/S2 site.
source: Whereas S2′ cleavage appears to be crucial for coronavirus infectivity, not all coronaviruses contain a multibasic S1/S2 site and little is known of its function (Hulswit et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: Until recently, all viruses within the clade of SARS-related viruses, including SARS-CoV, were found to lack a multibasic S1/S2 cleavage site.
source: Until recently, all viruses within the clade of SARS-related viruses, including SARS-CoV, were found to lack a multibasic S1/S2 cleavage site.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about SARS-related virus characteristics.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 contains a proline-arginine-arginine-alanine (PRRA) insertion into the S protein, creating a multibasic RRAR cleavage motif.
source: However, SARS-CoV-2 contains a proline-arginine-arginine-alanine (PRRA) insertion into the S protein, precisely N-terminally from a conserved arginine, creating a multibasic RRAR cleavage motif.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about the SARS-CoV-2 S protein structure.

claim: Exchanging the SARS-CoV-2 S MBCS for the SARS-CoV monobasic site decreases fusogenicity on VeroE6 cells.
source: Exchanging the SARS-CoV-2 S MBCS for the SARS-CoV monobasic site was recently shown to decrease fusogenicity on a monkey kidney cell line (VeroE6) and infectivity in a human lung adenocarcinoma cell line (Calu-3) (Hoffmann et al., 2020a; Shang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Exchanging the SARS-CoV-2 S MBCS for the SARS-CoV monobasic site decreases infectivity in Calu-3 cells.
source: Exchanging the SARS-CoV-2 S MBCS for the SARS-CoV monobasic site was recently shown to decrease fusogenicity on a monkey kidney cell line (VeroE6) and infectivity in a human lung adenocarcinoma cell line (Calu-3) (Hoffmann et al., 2020a; Shang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Entry of SARS-CoV-2 pseudoparticles into Calu-3 cells can be blocked using camostat mesylate.
source: Another study showed that entry of SARS-CoV-2 pseudoparticles (PP) into Calu-3 cells could be blocked using a clinically approved serine protease inhibitor (camostat mesylate) (Hoffmann et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: In most cell lines, SARS-CoV-2 entry appears to be mediated by endosomal cathepsins.
source: In contrast, in most other cell lines (including the lung cell line A549), recent CRISPR-Cas9 screens have suggested that SARS-CoV-2 entry in cell lines appears to be mediated by endosomal cathepsins (Daniloski et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2020a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to CRISPR-Cas9 screen studies.

claim: Wild-type and mutant SARS-CoV-2 pseudoparticles were produced at similar levels.
source: Immunoblotting revealed that wild-type and mutant PPs were produced at similar levels (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: S1/S2 cleavage was observed for the wild-type SARS-CoV-2 pseudoparticles.
source: S1/S2 cleavage was observed for the wild-type SARS-CoV-2 PPs and abrogated by the PRRA deletion and the R685A and R685H substitutions, which is in agreement with studies showing that the SARS-CoV-2 S is cleaved by proprotein convertases, possibly furin (Hoffmann et al., 2020a; Shang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citations to published studies.

claim: S1/S2 cleavage was abrogated by the PRRA deletion and the R685A and R685H substitutions.
source: S1/S2 cleavage was observed for the wild-type SARS-CoV-2 PPs and abrogated by the PRRA deletion and the R685A and R685H substitutions, which is in agreement with studies showing that the SARS-CoV-2 S is cleaved by proprotein convertases, possibly furin (Hoffmann et al., 2020a; Shang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citations to published studies.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 S is cleaved by proprotein convertases, possibly furin.
source: S1/S2 cleavage was observed for the wild-type SARS-CoV-2 PPs and abrogated by the PRRA deletion and the R685A and R685H substitutions, which is in agreement with studies showing that the SARS-CoV-2 S is cleaved by proprotein convertases, possibly furin (Hoffmann et al., 2020a; Shang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: SARS-2-Del-PRRA and SARS-2-R685A mutants were 5- to 10-fold more infectious on VeroE6 cells compared to wild-type.
source: Next, we assessed the infectivity of these viruses and found that the SARS-2-Del-PRRA and SARS-2-R685A mutants were 5- to 10-fold more infectious on VeroE6 cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by infectivity data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: On Calu-3 cells, SARS-2-Del-PRRA, SARS-2-R685A, and SARS-2-R685H pseudoparticles were approximately 5- to 10-fold less infectious compared with wild-type.
source: In contrast, on the lung adenocarcinoma cell line Calu-3, the SARS-2-Del-PRRA, SARS-2-R685A, and SARS-2-R685H PPs were approximately 5- to 10-fold less infectious compared with the wild-type PPs (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by infectivity data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The PRRA deletion and single point mutations functionally destroy the MBCS.
source: These data show that the PRRA deletion and single point mutations could functionally destroy the MBCS and suggest that this site enhances airway cell entry.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing loss of cleavage and altered infectivity.

claim: The MBCS enhances airway cell entry.
source: These data show that the PRRA deletion and single point mutations could functionally destroy the MBCS and suggest that this site enhances airway cell entry.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing altered infectivity patterns.

claim: Human airway organoid cultures express ACE2.
source: Moreover, they express the SARS-CoV-2 entry receptor angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) and transmembrane protease serine 2 (TMPRSS2), a serine protease previously shown to mediate SARS-CoV-2 entry when overexpressed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E; Hoffmann et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Human airway organoid cultures express TMPRSS2.
source: Moreover, they express the SARS-CoV-2 entry receptor angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) and transmembrane protease serine 2 (TMPRSS2), a serine protease previously shown to mediate SARS-CoV-2 entry when overexpressed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E; Hoffmann et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: TMPRSS2 mediates SARS-CoV-2 entry when overexpressed.
source: Moreover, they express the SARS-CoV-2 entry receptor angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) and transmembrane protease serine 2 (TMPRSS2), a serine protease previously shown to mediate SARS-CoV-2 entry when overexpressed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E; Hoffmann et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 pseudoparticles successfully infected human airway organoids.
source: SARS-CoV-2 PPs successfully infected these hAOs, as observed by fluorescent microscopy (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescent microscopy data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 pseudoparticles were approximately two times more infectious on human airway organoids compared with SARS-2-Del-PRRA and SARS-2-R685A mutants.
source: SARS-CoV-2 PPs were approximately two times more infectious on these cells compared with the SARS-2-Del-PRRA and SARS-2-R685A mutants, and eight times more infectious than the SARS-2-R685H mutant (Figure 1F), demonstrating that the SARS-CoV-2 MBCS facilitates entry into human airway cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by infectivity data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 pseudoparticles were eight times more infectious on human airway organoids than the SARS-2-R685H mutant.
source: SARS-CoV-2 PPs were approximately two times more infectious on these cells compared with the SARS-2-Del-PRRA and SARS-2-R685A mutants, and eight times more infectious than the SARS-2-R685H mutant (Figure 1F), demonstrating that the SARS-CoV-2 MBCS facilitates entry into human airway cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by infectivity data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 MBCS facilitates entry into human airway cells.
source: SARS-CoV-2 PPs were approximately two times more infectious on these cells compared with the SARS-2-Del-PRRA and SARS-2-R685A mutants, and eight times more infectious than the SARS-2-R685H mutant (Figure 1F), demonstrating that the SARS-CoV-2 MBCS facilitates entry into human airway cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing differential infectivity.

claim: SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2 pseudoparticles readily infected Calu-3 cells.
source: As SARS-CoV lacks the MBCS, we compared its infectivity to SARS-CoV-2 and found that both PPs readily infected Calu-3 cells, indicating that the SARS-CoV S has adaptations other than the MBCS to facilitate airway cell infection (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by infectivity data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: SARS-CoV S has adaptations other than the MBCS to facilitate airway cell infection.
source: As SARS-CoV lacks the MBCS, we compared its infectivity to SARS-CoV-2 and found that both PPs readily infected Calu-3 cells, indicating that the SARS-CoV S has adaptations other than the MBCS to facilitate airway cell infection (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that SARS-CoV infects Calu-3 cells despite lacking an MBCS.

claim: Inserting the PRRA motif into SARS-CoV S did not increase pseudoparticle infectivity on Calu-3 cells.
source: Likewise, inserting the PRRA motif into SARS-CoV S and thereby generating an MBCS did not increase PP infectivity on Calu-3 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by infectivity data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Entry of SARS-CoV-2 pseudoparticles into Calu-3 cells was not inhibited by E64D.
source: Entry of SARS-CoV-2 PPs was not inhibited by E64D, but could be inhibited by camostat, indicating that SARS-CoV-2 exclusively uses serine proteases for entry into these cells (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by inhibitor assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Entry of SARS-CoV-2 pseudoparticles into Calu-3 cells could be inhibited by camostat.
source: Entry of SARS-CoV-2 PPs was not inhibited by E64D, but could be inhibited by camostat, indicating that SARS-CoV-2 exclusively uses serine proteases for entry into these cells (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by inhibitor assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 exclusively uses serine proteases for entry into Calu-3 cells.
source: Entry of SARS-CoV-2 PPs was not inhibited by E64D, but could be inhibited by camostat, indicating that SARS-CoV-2 exclusively uses serine proteases for entry into these cells (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the inhibitor assay results.

claim: Entry of SARS-CoV pseudoparticles into Calu-3 cells was inhibited slightly by E64D (~10%).
source: For SARS-CoV PPs, entry was inhibited slightly by E64D (~10%), but camostat had a far stronger effect (~90%), indicating that SARS-CoV mainly uses serine proteases to enter Calu-3 cells but that a small fraction of virions enter via cathepsins (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by inhibitor assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Camostat inhibited SARS-CoV pseudoparticle entry into Calu-3 cells by ~90%.
source: For SARS-CoV PPs, entry was inhibited slightly by E64D (~10%), but camostat had a far stronger effect (~90%), indicating that SARS-CoV mainly uses serine proteases to enter Calu-3 cells but that a small fraction of virions enter via cathepsins (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by inhibitor assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: SARS-CoV mainly uses serine proteases to enter Calu-3 cells but a small fraction of virions enter via cathepsins.
source: For SARS-CoV PPs, entry was inhibited slightly by E64D (~10%), but camostat had a far stronger effect (~90%), indicating that SARS-CoV mainly uses serine proteases to enter Calu-3 cells but that a small fraction of virions enter via cathepsins (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the inhibitor assay results.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 entered faster than SARS-CoV via serine proteases into Calu-3 cells.
source: Using both PPs and authentic virus (Figure 2D,E), we observed that SARS-CoV-2 entered faster than SARS-CoV via serine proteases.
evidence: The claim is supported by entry kinetics data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: In contrast to SARS-CoV pseudoparticles, SARS-PRRA pseudoparticles were partially cleaved.
source: Immunoblotting revealed that, in contrast to SARS-CoV PPs, SARS-PRRA PPs were partially cleaved (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Wild-type SARS-CoV pseudoparticles used cathepsins for entry, whereas SARS-PRRA pseudoparticles did not.
source: Whereas wild-type SARS-CoV PPs used cathepsins, SARS-PRRA PPs did not (Figure 2H,I).
evidence: The claim is supported by inhibitor assay data shown in Figure 2H and 2I.

claim: The serine protease-mediated entry rate of SARS-PRRA pseudoparticles on Calu-3 cells was higher compared with SARS-CoV pseudoparticles.
source: The serine protease-mediated entry rate of SARS-PRRA PPs on Calu-3 cells was higher compared with SARS-CoV PPs (Figure 2J), and it was lower for SARS-2-Del-PRRA PPs compared with SARS-CoV-2 PPs (Figure 2K).
evidence: The claim is supported by entry kinetics data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The serine protease-mediated entry rate of SARS-2-Del-PRRA pseudoparticles was lower compared with SARS-CoV-2 pseudoparticles.
source: The serine protease-mediated entry rate of SARS-PRRA PPs on Calu-3 cells was higher compared with SARS-CoV PPs (Figure 2J), and it was lower for SARS-2-Del-PRRA PPs compared with SARS-CoV-2 PPs (Figure 2K).
evidence: The claim is supported by entry kinetics data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 MBCS facilitates serine protease-mediated entry on Calu-3 cells.
source: These findings show that the SARS-CoV-2 MBCS facilitates serine protease-mediated entry on Calu-3 cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing altered entry kinetics and protease usage.

claim: In HEK-293T cells, MBCS containing S proteins were more cleaved than S proteins without this site.
source: In HEK-293T cells, MBCS containing S proteins were more cleaved than S proteins without this site (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 S was more fusogenic than SARS-CoV S on Calu-3 cells.
source: We observed that SARS-CoV-2 S was more fusogenic than SARS-CoV S on Calu-3 cells (Figure 3B,C), VeroE6 cells, and VeroE6-TMPRSS2 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D and E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by fusion assay data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 S was more fusogenic than SARS-CoV S on VeroE6 cells.
source: We observed that SARS-CoV-2 S was more fusogenic than SARS-CoV S on Calu-3 cells (Figure 3B,C), VeroE6 cells, and VeroE6-TMPRSS2 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D and E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by fusion assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 S was more fusogenic than SARS-CoV S on VeroE6-TMPRSS2 cells.
source: We observed that SARS-CoV-2 S was more fusogenic than SARS-CoV S on Calu-3 cells (Figure 3B,C), VeroE6 cells, and VeroE6-TMPRSS2 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D and E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by fusion assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: The expression of TMPRSS2 increased fusion about twofold for both SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2 S proteins.
source: The expression of TMPRSS2 increased fusion about twofold for both S proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by fusion assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The insertion of the MBCS into SARS-CoV S increased fusion.
source: The insertion of the MBCS into SARS-CoV S increased fusion, whereas mutations in the SARS-CoV-2 S MBCS decreased fusion (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fusion assay data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Mutations in the SARS-CoV-2 S MBCS decreased fusion.
source: The insertion of the MBCS into SARS-CoV S increased fusion, whereas mutations in the SARS-CoV-2 S MBCS decreased fusion (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fusion assay data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 frequently induced syncytia in human airway organoids.
source: SARS-CoV-2 frequently induced syncytia, whereas SARS-CoV-infected cells rarely contained multiple nuclei (Figure 3D,E for quantification).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3D and quantification in Figure 3E.

claim: SARS-CoV-infected cells rarely contained multiple nuclei in human airway organoids.
source: SARS-CoV-2 frequently induced syncytia, whereas SARS-CoV-infected cells rarely contained multiple nuclei (Figure 3D,E for quantification).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3D and quantification in Figure 3E.

claim: VeroE6 cells have an active cathepsin-mediated cell entry pathway.
source: Therefore, we focused on VeroE6 cells, which have an active cathepsin-mediated cell entry pathway, as on these cells both SARS-CoV-2 PP and SARS-CoV PP entry was inhibited by E64D, and not by camostat (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by inhibitor assay data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: On VeroE6 cells, both SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV pseudoparticle entry was inhibited by E64D.
source: Therefore, we focused on VeroE6 cells, which have an active cathepsin-mediated cell entry pathway, as on these cells both SARS-CoV-2 PP and SARS-CoV PP entry was inhibited by E64D, and not by camostat (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by inhibitor assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: On VeroE6 cells, SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV pseudoparticle entry was not inhibited by camostat.
source: Therefore, we focused on VeroE6 cells, which have an active cathepsin-mediated cell entry pathway, as on these cells both SARS-CoV-2 PP and SARS-CoV PP entry was inhibited by E64D, and not by camostat (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by inhibitor assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In VeroE6-TMPRSS2 cells, SARS-CoV-2 pseudoparticle entry was inhibited ~95% by camostat.
source: In these cells, SARS-CoV-2 PP entry was inhibited ~95% by camostat, whereas SARS-CoV PPs were only inhibited ~35% (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by inhibitor assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In VeroE6-TMPRSS2 cells, SARS-CoV pseudoparticle entry was inhibited ~35% by camostat.
source: In these cells, SARS-CoV-2 PP entry was inhibited ~95% by camostat, whereas SARS-CoV PPs were only inhibited ~35% (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by inhibitor assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: E64D did not block SARS-CoV-2 pseudoparticle entry into VeroE6-TMPRSS2 cells.
source: In accordance, E64D did not block SARS-CoV-2 PP entry, while it decreased SARS-CoV PP entry ~30%.
evidence: The claim is supported by inhibitor assay data.

claim: E64D decreased SARS-CoV pseudoparticle entry into VeroE6-TMPRSS2 cells by ~30%.
source: In accordance, E64D did not block SARS-CoV-2 PP entry, while it decreased SARS-CoV PP entry ~30%.
evidence: The claim is supported by inhibitor assay data.

claim: Despite a functional serine protease-mediated entry pathway, a significant part of SARS-CoV pseudoparticles still retained cathepsin-mediated entry.
source: These findings indicate that despite a functional serine protease-mediated entry pathway, a significant part of SARS-CoV PPs still retained cathepsin-mediated entry, whereas SARS-CoV-2 PPs only used serine proteases for entry.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the inhibitor assay results.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 pseudoparticles only used serine proteases for entry into VeroE6-TMPRSS2 cells.
source: These findings indicate that despite a functional serine protease-mediated entry pathway, a significant part of SARS-CoV PPs still retained cathepsin-mediated entry, whereas SARS-CoV-2 PPs only used serine proteases for entry.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the inhibitor assay results.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 pseudoparticles containing mutations in the MBCS entered less through serine proteases and more through cathepsins.
source: This phenotype was found to be linked to the MBCS as SARS-CoV-2 PPs containing mutations in this site entered less through serine proteases and more through cathepsins (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by inhibitor assay data shown in Figure 4E and 4F.

claim: The introduction of the MBCS into SARS-CoV pseudoparticles increased serine protease usage while decreasing cathepsin usage.
source: In accordance, the introduction of the MBCS into SARS-CoV PPs increased serine proteases usage, while decreasing cathepsin usage (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by inhibitor assay data shown in Figure 4G and 4H.

claim: Camostat efficiently blocked SARS-CoV-2 infection in human airway organoids at 16 hours postinfection.
source: These cells were infected with SARS-CoV-2 at a high multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 2, but pretreatment with camostat efficiently blocked virus infection as evidenced by confocal microscopy on hAOs fixed at 16 hr postinfection (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Cathepsin inhibition did not affect SARS-CoV-2 entry into human airway organoids.
source: Cathepsin inhibition did not affect entry.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from inhibitor assays.

claim: At 24 hours postinfection, SARS-CoV-2 infection spread in human airway organoids treated with DMSO or E64D, but only rare single cells were observed after camostat treatment.
source: At 24 hr postinfection, SARS-CoV-2 infection spread in hAOs treated with dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) or E64D, but only rare single cells were observed after camostat treatment (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Camostat reduced SARS-CoV-2 replication in human airway organoids by approximately 90%.
